lesson.title: Splitting the Difference: The Midpoint Riemann Sum
lesson.summary: A midpoint Riemann sum evaluates the function at the center of each subinterval, and for smooth, curving functions it is typically far more accurate than either the left or right sum.
lesson.body:
A midpoint Riemann sum uses the midpoint of each subinterval, rather than either endpoint, as the sample point. If a subinterval runs from x_(i-1) to x_i, its midpoint is (x_(i-1)+x_i)/2. Using the midpoint tends to produce a much better approximation than either the left or right sum, because the rectangle's flat top is centered on the curve rather than pinned to whichever edge happens to be too high or too low.

Intuitively, over a single subinterval, a curving function sits a little above its midpoint rectangle's top on one side and a little below it on the other, and for a reasonably smooth curve those two errors roughly cancel rather than both pushing in the same direction the way left and right sum errors do. This is why, for the same number of subintervals, the midpoint sum usually beats both the left and right sums for accuracy, even though it takes no more work to compute.

Use the same f(x) = x² on the interval from 0 to 2, n = 4, Δx = 0.5. The subintervals are [0,0.5], [0.5,1.0], [1.0,1.5], [1.5,2.0], with midpoints 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, and 1.75. The function values there are f(0.25) = 0.0625, f(0.75) = 0.5625, f(1.25) = 1.5625, f(1.75) = 3.0625. The midpoint Riemann sum is Δx times [0.0625+0.5625+1.5625+3.0625] = 0.5 times 5.25 = 2.625.

Compare this to the exact value, 8/3, about 2.6667. The midpoint sum of 2.625 is off by only about 0.0417, far closer than the left sum's error of about 0.9167 or the right sum's error of about 1.0833 from the previous two chapters, using the exact same four rectangles and the exact same amount of arithmetic. This is the practical payoff of choosing the sample point wisely rather than defaulting to an endpoint.

The midpoint sum builds on the same general Riemann sum idea as the left and right sums, changing only which point in each subinterval supplies the height. It will reappear when you study numerical integration more formally, since it is one of the standard building blocks, alongside the trapezoidal rule covered next, for estimating integrals that do not have a clean antiderivative.
